Special relativity

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 16k Articles: 217
Special relativity describes physics in Minkowski spacetime, where inertial frames assign different space and time coordinates to the same spacetime events. Its two postulates are Einstein's principle of relativity and the same vacuum speed of light c in every inertial frame, independent of the source's motion. Together they replace the Galilean transformation with the Lorentz transformation, coupling space and time rather than providing a universal clock. Einstein's 1905 paper developed this account through measuring rods, clocks, and light signals. [ref].
A spacetime event is an occurrence at a definite place and time: a pulse reaching a detector, for example. An inertial frame supplies a Cartesian coordinate system and clocks at rest throughout it. Einstein synchronisation sets a distant clock's reflection reading to the midpoint between a light signal's departure and return readings at the sending clock. The resulting coordinate time records the local synchronized clock at each spacetime event; it differs from the time when a distant observer receives its image. This distinction makes time dilation, length contraction, and the relativity of simultaneity precise measurements. [ref].
The beauty of special relativity is that these different measurements fit one geometry: all inertial frames agree on the Minkowski interval. It lets us translate an experiment between a laboratory and a moving apparatus while preserving the light-signal relations between spacetime events.

Four-gradient (∂μ​=(c−1∂t​,∇))

Words: 47
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
For coordinates xμ=(ct,x,y,z), the four-gradient of a scalar field is its covector of coordinate derivatives. Under a constant Lorentz transformation, ∂μ′​=(Λ−1)νμ​∂ν​. In metric signature (+,−,−,−), raising its index gives ∂μ=(c−1∂t​,−∇). Contracting it with a four-vector field produces the Lorentz scalar four-divergence. In particular ∂μ​Jμ=0 is charge continuity in every inertial frame.

Relativistic beaming

Words: 198 Articles: 4
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Angular concentration and Doppler enhancement of radiation from a relativistically moving emitter. Frequency, photon arrival rate and apparent solid angle transform together; inferred brightness depends on viewing angle and the emission geometry.

Doppler boosting of a moving blob (Fν​=D3+αFν′​)

Words: 51
Relativistic beaming OurBigBook.com
For an unresolved, isotropically emitting rest-frame blob with power-law spectrum Fν′​∝ν−α, the observed spectral flux density at a fixed frequency is enhanced by D3+α. The factors follow from Lorentz-invariant specific intensity and the frequency shift. The bolometric or corresponding-logarithmic-bin luminosity transforms with D4. A spatially steady continuous jet has a different equal-arrival-time sampling and can have exponent 2+α instead.

Lorentz-invariant specific intensity (Iν​/ν3)

Words: 46
Relativistic beaming OurBigBook.com
The photon phase-space occupation is a Lorentz scalar. For radiation propagating through vacuum, this makes specific intensity divided by cubed frequency invariant under a change of inertial observer. With Doppler factor D, Iν​(ν)=D3Iν′′​(ν/D). This describes corresponding ray directions; it does not assert that an angularly integrated radiation field is isotropic in both frames.

Jet brightness asymmetry

Words: 45
Relativistic beaming OurBigBook.com
An approaching jet can be enhanced and its receding counterpart suppressed by different Doppler factors. A discrete moving emitter with rest-frame power-law spectrum Fν​∝ν−s has the usual boost δD3+s​, whereas a steady continuous-jet convention changes the exponent. Absorption and environmental asymmetry can also affect the contrast.

Doppler factor (δD​=[Γ(1−βcosθ)]−1)

Words: 26
Relativistic beaming OurBigBook.com
For velocity βc at angle θ toward the observer, δD​=[Γ(1−βcosθ)]−1. Frequencies transform as ν=δD​ν′ before cosmological redshift. Specific-intensity transformation follows invariance of Iν​/ν3.

Mass-energy equivalence (E0​=mc2)

Words: 42
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
The rest energy of a body is E0​=mc2. A body emitting energy dE and no net momentum in its rest frame loses mass dE/c2. For a radiating source of luminosity L, the corresponding radiative mass-loss rate is L/c2.

Postulates of special relativity

Words: 61
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
The first postulate is Einstein's principle of relativity: nongravitational laws have the same form in every inertial frame. The second states that light in vacuum propagates at the same finite speed of light c in every inertial frame, independently of the source's motion. Together with the usual spacetime symmetries and calibrated coordinates, these postulates yield the Lorentz transformation. The relativity principle alone also admits the Galilean transformation with its infinite invariant-speed limit.

Tests of special relativity

Words: 143 Articles: 2
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Special relativity connects measurable clock rates, length contraction, light propagation, and four-momentum through the Lorentz transformation. Tests probe particular predictions rather than measuring a coordinate transformation in isolation. Examples include cosmic-ray muon time-dilation experiments, muon storage-ring time-dilation experiments, the Michelson-Morley experiment, the Fizeau experiment, and particle-collision energy and momentum balances.

Bertozzi's electron speed-energy experiment

Words: 46
Tests of special relativity OurBigBook.com
William Bertozzi compared electron time-of-flight speeds with independently measured kinetic energies using electrostatic and linear acceleration. The 1964 report covers 0.5–15 MeV and uses calorimetry to check deposited energy. Speed approaches the light-speed limit while energy continues rising, testing relativistic energy against an unrestricted Newtonian extrapolation.[ref]

Michelson-Morley experiment

Words: 60
Tests of special relativity OurBigBook.com
An interferometer compares round-trip light travel times along perpendicular arms as its orientation changes. The absence of the classical stationary-aether fringe shift at the expected scale constrains orientation dependence of the round-trip speed of light. The result is consistent with special relativity, but alone does not select it uniquely from every alternative theory.[ref]

Thomas precession

Words: 68
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Thomas precession is the kinematic rotation arising when the successive instantaneous rest frames of an accelerated particle are connected by noncollinear Lorentz boosts. Its contribution is needed in deriving the leading atomic spin-orbit coupling: for an electron in central potential energy U(r), the corrected term is Hso​=[2me2​c2r]−1(dU/dr)L⋅S. A rest-field argument alone gives twice this coefficient.[ref]

Relativistic force transformation (F⊥​=F⊥′​/γ)

Words: 66
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
For a particle instantaneously at rest in a primed frame moving at vx relative to the laboratory, the ordinary three-force transforms as F∥​=F∥′​ and F⊥​=F⊥′​/γ. The spatial components of the four-force are γu​F, whereas its time component is γu​F⋅u/c. For a co-moving material segment, length contraction also changes its laboratory length, so transforming total force is not the same as transforming force per unit length.

Einstein's principle of relativity

Words: 107 Articles: 1
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
The laws of physics have the same form in all inertial frames; uniform absolute motion cannot be identified by experiments confined to an inertial laboratory. The invariant vacuum speed of light is a separate postulate. Together they motivate the Lorentz transformations of special relativity.

Einstein synchronisation

Words: 67
Einstein's principle of relativity OurBigBook.com
Einstein synchronisation sets clocks at rest in one inertial frame using exchanged light signals. If the sending clock records departure at tA​ and return at tA′​, the distant clock's reflection reading is set to tB​=(tA​+tA′​)/2. This convention assigns equal outgoing and incoming travel times and defines the frame's distant simultaneity. It does not set the arrival time of an image equal to the time of the remote spacetime event.

Relativistic particle (uμuμ​=c2)

Words: 38
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
A relativistic massive particle is described by a timelike worldline with proper-time four-velocity uμ. In signature (+−−−) its normalization is uμuμ​=c2 and its momentum is pμ=muμ. The relativistic charged-particle action adds electromagnetic coupling, whose variation gives the Lorentz force.

Nonrelativistic particle

Words: 30
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
A massive particle is nonrelativistic when its speed is small compared with the speed of light. Its energy expansion is E=mc2+p2/(2m)+O(p4/(m3c2)). The leading momentum-dependent term is the classical kinetic energy.

Hyperbolic motion (x2−c2t2=c2t02​)

Words: 141 Articles: 2
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Hyperbolic motion in special relativity is rectilinear motion with constant proper acceleration. A representative positive-x world line is x=ct0​cosh(τ/t0​), t=t0​sinh(τ/t0​), with proper acceleration c/t0​. This describes a hyperbola in spacetime, not a hyperbolic Kepler orbit.

Hyperbolic motion from an initial event and rapidity (η(τ)=η0​+aτ)

Words: 48
Hyperbolic motion OurBigBook.com
In units c=1, constant signed proper acceleration a gives
t−t0​=asinh(η0​+aτ)−sinhη0​​,x−x0​=acosh(η0​+aτ)−coshη0​​.
(1)
Position data determine t0​,x0​ but leave the initial rapidity η0​ free. Proper-acceleration magnitude alone also leaves its orientation unspecified. The familiar centred hyperbola x2−t2=a−2 follows for the additional initial data t0​=0, x0​=1/a, η0​=0 and acceleration toward increasing x.

Finite-acceleration correction to a relativistic cruise (Δτ=(2c/a)[η−(coshη−1)/sinhη])

Words: 61
Hyperbolic motion OurBigBook.com
Replace instantaneous acceleration and braking by legs of constant proper-acceleration magnitude a, retaining the same cruise rapidity η and fixed endpoint separation. Each leg takes proper time cη/a and displaces (c2/a)(coshη−1) in the endpoint rest frame. Subtracting the proper cruise time displaced by both legs gives the displayed correction. A cruise segment exists only if the total endpoint separation exceeds twice this acceleration distance.

Proper length (ℓ)

Words: 32
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Proper length is spatial length measured using the induced metric on a specified spacelike slice. For a moving extended object, specify the simultaneity convention; local rest lengths need not coincide with a coordinate length.

Spacetime

Words: 361 Articles: 6
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Spacetime combines spatial position and time into one geometric setting for physical events. In special relativity it is modeled by Minkowski spacetime; in general relativity its geometry is dynamical.

Event (relativity)

Words: 49
Spacetime OurBigBook.com
A spacetime event is an idealized occurrence at one point of spacetime, such as a light pulse reaching a detector. An inertial frame assigns spatial coordinates and a time coordinate to it. Different frames can assign different coordinates to the same spacetime event; the event itself is not changed by a coordinate transformation.

Spacetime extension

Words: 159 Articles: 2
Spacetime OurBigBook.com
A spacetime extension is an isometric embedding of a spacetime as a proper open subset of a larger connected spacetime with a nondegenerate Lorentzian metric. The allowed differentiability class must be specified: analytic, smooth and low-regularity extensions are different questions. Divergent curvature can obstruct a regular extension even when an incomplete geodesic has finite affine length.

Maximal analytic extension

Words: 57
Spacetime extension OurBigBook.com
A maximal analytic extension of an analytic spacetime is an analytic spacetime extension admitting no further proper analytic extension as a regular spacetime of the same dimension. It is different from a maximal Cauchy development, which can end at a smooth Cauchy horizon. Additional global choices or quotients can affect uniqueness. The simply connected extension of positive-mass Schwarzschild spacetime through both horizons is the Kruskal spacetime; its curvature singularities remain boundaries.

Extendible spacetime

Words: 48
Spacetime extension OurBigBook.com
An extendible spacetime admits a spacetime extension in the specified regularity class. A coordinate horizon need not obstruct an extension: the exterior Schwarzschild chart extends through its horizon in regular null coordinates. Maximality refers to extensions of the given spacetime, not to the mere absence of a singularity in one coordinate chart.

Proper time (τ)

Words: 129 Articles: 1
Spacetime OurBigBook.com
Proper time is the time measured by a clock following a timelike worldline. With metric signature (−,+,+,+) and units c=1,
dτ2=−ds2
(2)
along that worldline.
Restoring the speed of light, the same metric signature gives dτ=−ds2​/c=dt1−∣v∣2/c2​ for a future-directed timelike curve. Integrating along a clock's world line gives its elapsed proper time, even when its velocity varies. For uniform motion this becomes the time dilation formula; it is not generally the square root of the interval between endpoints of a curved world line.

Proper lifetime inferred from a delayed decay flash (τ=treceive​(1−β)/(1+β)​)

Words: 57
Proper time OurBigBook.com
An inertial particle passes a stationary detector, then recedes at speed v=βc before decaying. The detector's reception time obeys treceive​=td​+vtd​/c. Dividing the decay time td​ by its Lorentz factor gives the title formula for elapsed proper time. A reception event at the detector and a decay event at the particle are not interchangeable endpoints for a time-dilation calculation.

Null vector

Words: 141 Articles: 2
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
A nonzero spacetime vector k is null when its Minkowski norm vanishes, kaka​=0. Null tangent vectors describe the local directions of light rays.
Special relativity describes inertial frames using Lorentz transformations and Minkowski spacetime.

Sum of future-pointing null vectors ((A+B)2=−2ab(1−n⋅m))

Words: 64
Null vector OurBigBook.com
In Minkowski spacetime with metric signature (−,+,+,+), write two nonzero future-pointing null vectors as A=a(1,n) and B=b(1,m), where a,b>0 and n,m are unit vectors. Their Lorentzian inner product gives
(A+B)⋅(A+B)=−2ab(1−n⋅m)≤0.
(3)
Thus their sum is a future-pointing causal vector. It is a null vector exactly when the spatial directions coincide, and a timelike vector otherwise. The positivity of the time components is essential: adding past- and future-pointing null vectors can instead produce a spacelike vector.

Null condition (g(k,k)=0)

Words: 42
Null vector OurBigBook.com
The null condition for a nonzero vector k in a Lorentzian metric is g(k,k)=0. Applied to the tangent of a curve it makes the curve a null curve. Nullity alone does not imply the geodesic equation; an additional zero or tangent-parallel covariant acceleration is required.

Lorentz factor (γ)

Words: 3k Articles: 17
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
For a relative speed 0≤v<c, the Lorentz factor is
γ=1−v2/c2​1​.
(4)
At v=0.6c, γ=1/1−0.36​=1/0.8=1.25. Thus a moving clock accumulates 0.8 seconds of proper time per laboratory second, and a parallel moving rod has 0.8 times its rest length. The Lorentz factor approaches one at small speed and grows without bound as v approaches the speed of light; a massive object's rest frame never requires a boost at v=c.

Length contraction (L=L0​/γ)

Words: 218 Articles: 1
Lorentz factor OurBigBook.com
A rod of rest length L0​ moving parallel to its length has simultaneous laboratory length L=L0​/γ, where γ is the Lorentz factor. Here L0​ is the rod's proper length measured in its rest frame. Transverse lengths are unchanged by the corresponding Lorentz transformation.
For a rod at rest in S′ with endpoints x′=0 and x′=10m, let S′ move at v=0.6c relative to the laboratory S. Record both endpoint positions at laboratory time t=0. The Lorentz transformation then gives x′=1.25x, so their recorded positions are 0 and 8m: the laboratory length is 10/1.25=8m. This is an operational definition: synchronized laboratory detectors register the endpoints at the same laboratory time. A photograph collects light emitted at different times and need not show this length. [ref].
For those same two endpoint spacetime events, Δt′=−1.25(0.6c)(8m)/c2=−6m/c. Thus the front-end measurement occurs earlier in S′ by about 20ns. Length contraction compares simultaneous endpoint measurements in each frame, which select different pairs of spacetime events; it does not mean that the rod has been compressed in its own rest frame.

Small-speed length contraction estimate

Words: 34
Length contraction OurBigBook.com
At speed v≪c, an endpoint separation L measured simultaneously in its own rest frame becomes L1−v2/c2​ in the moving frame, shorter by approximately Lv2/(2c2). The stable evaluation Lβ2/[1+1−β2​] avoids subtracting nearly equal floating-point numbers.

Time dilation (Δt=γΔτ)

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Lorentz factor OurBigBook.com
If one clock measures a proper time interval Δτ while moving at constant speed v in an inertial frame, that frame measures Δt=γΔτ, where γ is the Lorentz factor. The two spacetime events must lie on that clock's world line.
Suppose a clock moving at 0.6c advances by 4μs between two ticks. Set t=x=t′=x′=0 at the first tick. The laboratory's synchronized clocks assign Δt=1.25×4=5μs. During that interval the clock travels Δx=0.6c×5μs=3cμs, approximately 899.38m. The Minkowski interval checks the result:
s2=−c2(5μs)2+(3cμs)2=−c2(4μs)2.
(5)
Both frames therefore recover the same 4μs of proper time. This calculation is useful whenever a process is timed on a moving apparatus but described using laboratory clocks.
A light clock makes the mechanism visible. Two mirrors separated by h perpendicular to the motion exchange a pulse; define one tick as its complete return to the lower mirror. In the clock's rest frame the tick takes Δτ=2h/c. In the laboratory each half-tick lasts T and the light traverses a diagonal, so the Pythagorean theorem gives
(cT)2=h2+(vT)2,T=γh/c,Δt=2T=γΔτ.
(6)
For h=1m and v=0.6c, each leg covers 1.25m while the mirrors move 0.75m. The return tick lasts 2.5m/c instead of 2m/c: the light has the same speed of light in both accounts. [ref].
Reciprocal time dilation is consistent: each inertial frame times the other frame's single moving clock using its own synchronized clock network. These comparisons use different simultaneous spacetime events. Comparing reunited clocks instead requires their complete world lines, as in the twin paradox.

Muon storage-ring time-dilation experiment

Words: 63
Time dilation OurBigBook.com
Accelerator-produced muons circulating in a magnetic storage ring allow a direct comparison between their measured laboratory mean lifetime and γ times the rest lifetime. The 1977 experiment at γ=29.33 measured positive- and negative-muon lifetimes near 64.4μs, consistent with time dilation. This is a controlled complement to atmospheric survival measurements, with different systematic effects.[ref]

Cosmic-ray muon time-dilation experiment

Words: 165 Articles: 1
Time dilation OurBigBook.com
Atmospheric cosmic rays generate muons whose mean lifetime at rest is about 2.2μs. Twin paradox

Time dilation OurBigBook.com
The twin paradox compares proper time along the different world lines of a travelling observer and a stay-at-home observer who reunite. Reciprocal inertial time dilation produces an apparent contradiction only if the traveller's change of inertial frame is ignored.
The decisive experiment is local: put two clocks together at departure, separate them, then compare their readings together at reunion. Everyone agrees on those two spacetime events and on the final difference. The twin paradox asks why two clocks can accumulate different proper times between the same spacetime events, despite reciprocal time dilation during uniform motion. Its answer is the geometry of their complete world lines, together with the relativity of simultaneity when comparing distant clocks.

The clock hypothesis says that an ideal clock following a timelike curve measures its proper time: its instantaneous rate depends on velocity through dτ=dt1−v2/c2​, with no separate acceleration term. Twin paradox clock experiments
Words: 988 Articles: 4
Twin paradox OurBigBook.com
The 1972 paper Around-the-World Atomic Clocks: Observed Relativistic Time Gains by J. C. Hafele and others reports four cesium-beam atomic clocks flown around the world in October 1971, eastward and westward. Their readings were compared with the U.S. Naval Observatory reference time scale before and after travel. An electronic time-interval counter resolved differences to the nearest nanosecond; intercomparisons among the flying clocks continued during travel. The final ensemble results were −59±10ns eastward and +273±7ns westward; the quoted spreads are standard deviations. These are corrected clock offsets, not raw readings or aircraft travel times. Four clocks allowed identification of individual rate changes through patterns in their mutual differences. The authors also report magnetic shielding and laboratory orientation checks. Their analysis could not detect a disturbance common to every flying clock, and the small ensemble limits statistical conclusions. This is a concrete reunited-clock experiment with apparatus, readout and drift controls.[ref]
The companion paper Around-the-World Atomic Clocks: Predicted Relativistic Time Gains by J. C. Hafele and others computes −40±23ns eastward and +275±21ns westward from the recorded flight paths. These are predictions, with flight-data uncertainty estimates. Both time dilation from motion and gravitational time dilation matter: aircraft clocks at altitude experience a different gravitational potential, while the rotating Earth means a ground clock is not the inertial home clock of our simple model. Eastward and westward motion change the aircraft's velocity relative to an approximately nonrotating inertial frame, not merely its speed relative to the ground. The measured agreement therefore tests combined special relativity and general relativity; the westward gain does not contradict the maximum-proper time result for fixed endpoints in Minkowski spacetime.[ref]
A complementary microscopic test is Measurements of relativistic time dilatation for positive and negative muons in a circular orbit by J. Bailey and others. The authors measured muon decay lifetimes in a storage ring at Lorentz factor γ=29.33: 64.419±0.058μs for positive muons and 64.368±0.029μs for negative muons. The reported positive-muon lifetime agrees with the independently measured lifetime at rest and special relativity to a fractional error of 2×10−3 at 95% confidence. This is a decay-lifetime readout under continuous centripetal acceleration, rather than a reunion of portable clocks. It supports the clock hypothesis for this physical process and regime; the inspected abstract does not establish universal immunity of every clock mechanism to acceleration. [ref]

Velocity-addition formula

Words: 2k Articles: 7
Lorentz transformation OurBigBook.com
The velocity-addition formula translates a particle's velocity between two specified inertial frames. Let S′ move at signed velocity V along the x-axis of S, with parallel axes and ∣V∣<c, where c is the speed of light. Define ux​=dx/dt and ux′​=dx′/dt′ for the same particle's world line, using position and time measured within the corresponding inertial frame. With Lorentz factor γV​=(1−V2/c2)−1/2, the forward Lorentz boost gives
ux′​=1−Vux​/c2ux​−V​,uy′​=γV​(1−Vux​/c2)uy​​,uz′​=γV​(1−Vux​/c2)uz​​.
(30)
For collinear motion, write u=ux​ and u′=ux′​. The inverse velocity-addition formula is
u=1+Vu′/c2u′+V​.
(31)
This is the composition of the particle's velocity in S′ and that frame's velocity relative to S. The velocities must belong to this same chain of reference frames, with directions specified. Two arbitrary quoted speeds cannot be inserted blindly. Each velocity measurement uses distances and clocks in a single inertial frame, with Einstein synchronisation for separated clocks.
For example, let V=0.6c and let the particle travel at u′=0.6c in S′. Its velocity in S is
u=1+0.6×0.60.6c+0.6c​=1715​c≈0.88235294c.
(32)
The Galilean transformation would instead give u=u′+V=1.2c, which fails here. For light moving along the positive axis, u′=c gives u=c; u′=−c similarly gives u=−c. Negative directions also work for massive particles: at V=0.6c, u′=−0.6c gives u=0, while u′=−0.8c gives u=−5c/13. Thus “addition” means composition of signed velocities, rather than addition of their magnitudes.
A short derivation differentiates the Lorentz transformation: dx′=γV​(dx−Vdt) and dt′=γV​(dt−Vdx/c2). Dividing these differentials gives the longitudinal velocity-addition formula. The transverse formulas use dy′=dy and dz′=dz, but the same transformed time denominator; omitting it would ignore the relativity of simultaneity. Replacing V by −V gives the inverse. When both relative and particle velocities are small compared with the speed of light, the denominator is close to one and the nonrelativistic limit recovers the Galilean transformation.
The formula lets us compare particle motion in a moving apparatus and a laboratory without losing the invariant speed of light. Einstein's 1905 paper derives the coordinate change in §3 and the composition of velocities in §5, including the collinear formula, its light-speed case, and composition of parallel transformations. [ref]. The rapidity parametrization makes the collinear composition particularly simple.

Fizeau experiment

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Velocity-addition formula OurBigBook.com
In 1851 Hippolyte Fizeau detected a change in light propagation through moving water using interference fringes. Sunlight entered a telescope through a partially reflecting mirror; two slits selected beams passing through parallel glass tubes, each 1.487m long with 5.3mm internal diameter. A second telescope and focal mirror exchanged the tubes on return, and the beams recombined at a graduated eyepiece. Compressed air drove water between reservoirs, producing opposite flows; reversing both flows reversed the interference fringe displacement. The double transit suppressed static differences in temperature and pressure; filling only one tube with water tested this compensation. Separate supports reduced mechanical disturbance. Hippolyte Fizeau estimated flow speed from volumetric flow rate divided by tube cross section.[ref]
The Fizeau experiment turns a tiny change in phase velocity into a visible fraction of an interference fringe. The Fizeau experiment path-length convention below explains why both tube passages contribute with the same sign for one beam and the opposite sign for the other. This makes the apparatus sensitive to the part of the phase difference that reverses with the flow, while rejecting disturbances shared by both beams.
Fresnel drag coefficient (f=1−n−2)
Words: 200
Fizeau experiment OurBigBook.com
The Fresnel drag coefficient is the factor f=1−1/n2 multiplying a transparent medium's velocity in the first-order change of collinear light phase velocity, when optical dispersion is neglected. Here n is the medium's refractive index in its rest frame. The name recalls Augustin Jean Fresnel's partial-drag law; special relativity obtains the same coefficient from the velocity-addition formula without introducing a luminiferous aether.
Let the water move at signed velocity u along the positive laboratory axis, with ∣u∣≪c/n, where c is the vacuum speed of light. Assume a transparent medium with constant n>1, uniform flow and negligible optical dispersion. In the water's local rest frame, a collinear constant-phase surface travels at v′=c/n. Dividing the Lorentz transformation differentials along that surface gives the same longitudinal velocity-addition formula as for a particle:
vlab​=1+u/(nc)c/n+u​=(nc​+u)(1−ncu​+O(c2u2​))=nc​+u(1−n21​)+O(cu2​).
(35)
The correction comes from the transformed time denominator. Simply adding u to c/n would omit it. This argument concerns collinear phase velocity; in a medium with optical dispersion, group velocity is a different quantity.[ref]
For n=4/3, the Fresnel drag coefficient is f=7/16. A chosen flow speed of 6ms−1 therefore changes the forward phase velocity by approximately 2.625ms−1, even though the stationary-medium phase velocity is about 2.25×108ms−1. These are model values. The invariant vacuum speed of light remains c; c/n describes propagation through matter in its own rest frame.
Fizeau experiment path-length convention (L=2ℓ)
Words: 371
Fizeau experiment OurBigBook.com
Use the schematic below to count the water traversals explicitly. Each stationary tube has laboratory length ℓ. In the displayed setting, upper-tube water flows right and lower-tube water flows left, each at speed u>0. Beam A goes right through the upper tube, exchanges tubes at the far optics, and returns left through the lower tube: it follows the flow twice. Beam B goes right through the lower tube and returns left through the upper tube: it opposes the flow twice. Each complete beam path therefore contains total water length L=2ℓ, not ℓ or 4ℓ. The connecting air paths and fixed optics are assumed to contribute no flow-dependent phase difference.
Let v+​ and v−​ be positive phase velocity magnitudes along and against the water flow:
v+​=1+u/(nc)c/n+u​,v−​=1−u/(nc)c/n−u​,Δt=tB​−tA​=L(v−​1​−v+​1​).
(36)
For a laboratory source of frequency ν=c/λ0​, where λ0​ is its vacuum wavelength, define the signed interference fringe offset N by the propagation phase difference Δϕ=2πνΔt=2πN. This is an equivalent phase delay between steady beams; no stopwatch resolves their transit-time difference. Subtract the zero-flow baseline and expand to first order:
Δt≃c22Lu​(n2−1)=c24ℓu​(n2−1),N(u)≃cλ0​2Lu​(n2−1)=cλ0​4ℓu​(n2−1).
(37)
Thus one shifted fringe corresponds to one cycle of phase difference. If the stationary pattern has spatial interference fringe spacing d, a simple readout model is I(x)=I0​[1+Vcos(2πx/d+2πN)], where V is the interference visibility. The maxima shift by −dN with this choice of screen coordinate. A sign assigned to “rightward” motion depends on the image orientation; the magnitude in fringe units does not.
Reversing both flows gives N(−u)=−N(u). The displacement between equal and opposite settings therefore has magnitude
∣N(u)−N(−u)∣=2∣N(u)∣≃cλ0​8ℓ∣u∣​(n2−1).
(38)
The factor 2 from comparing opposite flows is additional to the factor 2 already included in L=2ℓ. Repeating a round trip in just one flowing tube would instead put a beam with the flow once and against it once; that geometry does not produce the two same-sign contributions drawn here.
Fizeau experiment worked example
Words: 399
Fizeau experiment OurBigBook.com
Choose ℓ=1.50m, n=4/3, λ0​=550nm and u=6.00ms−1, with c=299792458ms−1. These are illustrative choices, not measured values or a reconstruction of Hippolyte Fizeau's data. Each beam traverses L=3.00m of water. The nondispersive prediction is
N=(299792458)(550×10−9)4(1.50)(6.00)(7/9)​≃0.16981,2N≃0.33963,Δt≃3.1154×10−16s.
(39)
The first number is the offset from rest to one flow setting; the second compares equal opposite settings. The very short equivalent delay explains why interference is useful: a measurable fraction of a wavelength replaces an unattainable direct timing measurement.
The Galilean transformation would give phase velocity magnitudes c/n±u, hence Nfull​≃4ℓun2/(cλ0​). At the chosen values this is 0.38815 fringe from rest, larger than the special relativity prediction by n2/(n2−1)=16/7. A model with no flow-induced change of phase velocity instead gives N=0. The three alternatives are experimentally distinguishable even when u/c is tiny.
Hippolyte Fizeau's positive displacement favoured Augustin Jean Fresnel's partial-drag law over zero or full drag. He explicitly distinguished support for that law from establishing its underlying luminiferous aether hypothesis.[ref] The Fizeau experiment therefore supplies a nonzero relative-motion measurement, not a null test proving an luminiferous aether's absence. The derivation above exhibits the same first-order law within special relativity, showing why agreement with the coefficient alone cannot select an physical interpretation.
Two limitations matter for precision. The velocity profile sampled by the beam need not equal the cross-sectional average inferred from volumetric flow rate. Also, the Doppler effect gives opposite rest-frame frequencies for the counterpropagating beams. With optical dispersion, the coefficient n2−1 in the interference fringe formula becomes
n2−1+nωdωdn​=n2−1−nλ0​dλ0​dn​,
(40)
where the refractive index and its derivative are evaluated for stationary water at the laboratory angular frequency ω=2πc/λ0​. A wavelength-independent n therefore defines an approximation, not a precision fit to real water.[ref] Flow reversal removes a fixed phase difference, but a mechanical or temperature change that reverses with the flow can still imitate the signal and must be controlled.

Sagnac effect (Δt≃4Ω⋅A/c2)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
The Sagnac effect is a difference in return times, or an associated interference fringe displacement, for light sent in opposite directions around a closed optical path in a rotating apparatus. The light leaves one beam splitter, travels around the same loop in opposite senses, and returns to the rotating beam splitter and readout. For a slowly rotating apparatus in flat spacetime, the leading laboratory arrival-time difference is
Δt=t+​−t−​≃c24Ω⋅A​,A=21​∮C​r×dr.
(41)
Here c is the vacuum speed of light, Ω is the apparatus's angular velocity relative to an inertial frame, and A is the vector area oriented by the chosen positive direction around the closed curve C. With positive rotation about the upward normal vector, the counterclockwise beam is labelled + and arrives later. Reversing rotation, or reversing the orientation convention alone, changes the sign of Δt.
The surprise is that a small loop can reveal its rotation by comparing two beams locally, even though each local vacuum speed of light measurement gives c. A rotating reference frame is not a single inertial frame: a beam must catch the moving receiver after a full circuit. The Sagnac area law makes this difference a practical way to measure angular velocity, while the Relativistic Sagnac delay on a circular ring distinguishes laboratory coordinate time from the receiver's proper time.

Sagnac interferometer

Words: 325 Articles: 1
Sagnac effect OurBigBook.com
A Sagnac interferometer uses a beam splitter to send light with optical coherence around a common closed optical path in opposite directions, then recombines the beams to read their phase difference. Mirrors or a guiding path define the loop; the source, beam splitter, loop and readout rotate together in the basic experiment. A small relative beam tilt makes spatial interference fringes whose displacement reveals a change of phase difference. At one fixed output, a photodetector can instead record the corresponding change in light intensity.

Sagnac interferometer OurBigBook.com
In 1913 Georges Sagnac mounted a lamp, collimator, beam splitter, four mirrors and photographic plate on a horizontal rotating platform. The mirrors defined a closed polygon; the two beams traversed it in opposite senses. A slight beam splitter adjustment produced visible interference fringes. A motor brought the platform to steady rotation, and switching the lamp exposed the plate. Comparing opposite senses of rotation revealed a reversing displacement. Changing the beam splitter adjustment supplied a further check against optical deformation. The report compared measured and calculated displacements. Georges Sagnac interpreted this as evidence for a luminiferous aether; the relativistic derivation below reproduces the delay without that hypothesis.[ref]
The readout measures a relative wave phase, not two stopwatch readings separated by an optical transit time. Reversal isolates a contribution odd in angular velocity: if a signed interference fringe position is q(Ω)=q0​+kΩ to leading order, then [q(Ω)−q(−Ω)]/2=kΩ cancels the fixed offset q0​. Changes of alignment or temperature correlated with reversal can survive this subtraction. Thus the experimental inference concerns a reproducible rotating-loop phase difference, with controls for disturbances; it is not by itself a unique test of an underlying propagation hypothesis.

Sagnac area law (Δt≃(2/c2)∮C​v⋅dr=4Ω⋅A/c2)

Words: 533 Articles: 1
Sagnac effect OurBigBook.com
For a rigidly rotating prescribed vacuum path, use spatial coordinates attached to the apparatus and laboratory time t. At a path point r, the local apparatus velocity is v=Ω×r. A light displacement has instantaneous laboratory displacement dr+vdt, up to the common rotation of the spatial axes. The null condition is therefore
c2dt2=∣dr+vdt∣2.
(42)
Write dℓ=∣dr∣. To first order in ∣v∣/c, the positive root is
dt≃cdℓ​+c2v⋅dr​.
(43)
Reversing the path reverses the dot product term but leaves the leading path-length term unchanged. Subtract the two return times and use the scalar triple product identity:
Δt≃c22​∮C​(Ω×r)⋅dr=c22​Ω⋅∮C​r×dr=c24Ω⋅A​.
(44)
This is a line integral version of the Sagnac area law; the vector area identity also follows from Stokes theorem. For a mirror-defined polygon the actual ray paths move slightly as the mirrors rotate; the stationary optical path at zero rotation gives the same first-order result. The prescribed-path calculation is an idealization, not an exact finite-speed formula for every moving-mirror layout.
The dot product explains the geometry: only the projection of the oriented vector area along the angular velocity contributes. A planar loop whose normal vector is perpendicular to Ω has zero leading delay. For repeated traversals with the same orientation, the signed vector areas add; oppositely oriented lobes can cancel even when the total unsigned area is large. Equal perimeter alone does not imply equal response. A constant translational velocity contributes nothing to this leading closed-path line integral, since ∮C​dr=0.

Sagnac fringe shift worked example (N≃4Ω⋅A/(cλ0​))

Sagnac area law OurBigBook.com
For a stationary rotating apparatus driven by a source with optical coherence and proper frequency ν0​, define λ0​=c/ν0​. The source wave phase advances by 2πν0​Δτ between the emission times of the two contributions that meet at one readout spacetime event. Define the signed phase lag Δϕ of the + contribution and the corresponding displacement N in units of one interference fringe by
Δϕ=2πν0​Δτ,N=2πΔϕ​≃cλ0​4Ω⋅A​.
(45)
The sign of a photographed spatial displacement also depends on the imposed fringe orientation; this definition fixes the theoretical sign through the delayed beam. In an equal-amplitude output, a representative light intensity is I(x)=Imax​[1+cos(Kx−Δϕ)]/2, where K sets the chosen spatial interference fringe spacing 2π/K. Moving Δϕ by 2π shifts the pattern by one fringe. A fixed output exactly at a bright or dark fringe has zero first-order intensity slope, so a known phase bias or a spatial fringe readout is useful for determining a small signed delay.
Choose a square of side 0.30m, a rectangle 0.40m by 0.20m, λ0​=633nm and Ω=+10rads−1, with angular velocity parallel to the positive normal vectors. Both perimeters are 1.20m, but the areas are 0.090m2 and 0.080m2. Using c=299792458ms−1, the leading predictions are
Δtsquare​Δtrectangle​​≃4.006×10−17s,≃3.560×10−17s,​Nsquare​Nrectangle​​≃0.0189705,≃0.0168626.​
(46)
These are original model choices and predictions, not measured points. The square has 9/8 times the response despite the equal path lengths. Reversing from +Ω to −Ω gives N(−Ω)−N(+Ω)=−2N(+Ω): the displacement magnitude between opposite rotations is twice the displacement magnitude from rest. Confusing these two comparisons introduces a factor-of-two error.

Relativistic Sagnac delay on a circular ring (Δτ=4ΩA/(c21−Ω2R2/c2​))

Sagnac effect OurBigBook.com
Consider an ideal circular vacuum path of laboratory radius R, a limit of closely spaced mirrors constraining light around the circle at laboratory speed c. The source and detector rotate uniformly together with signed angular velocity Ω, where ∣Ω∣R<c, in flat spacetime. Let L=2πR be the laboratory circumference and A=πR2 the positive area. The + pulse travels counterclockwise and the − pulse clockwise, independently of the sign of Ω. Both depart from the detector at t=0.
Unwrap the circle into a laboratory arc coordinate. The two first-return conditions are
ct+​=L+ΩRt+​,ct−​=L−ΩRt−​.
(47)
Consequently the exact laboratory arrival times and their difference are
t+​=c−ΩRL​,t−​=c+ΩRL​,Δt=c2−Ω2R24ΩA​.
(48)
The denominators c∓ΩR are closing rates in these laboratory equations; they are not local speed of light measurements by a rotating observer. The two arrival spacetime events lie on the same detector world line. Its constant speed is ∣Ω∣R, so proper time along that world line gives
Δτ=1−c2Ω2R2​​Δt=c21−Ω2R2/c2​4ΩA​.
(49)
Thus laboratory coordinate-time and rotating-detector proper time delays agree only to leading order at small ∣Ω∣R/c. The radius and circumference here are laboratory quantities, not lengths obtained by laying comoving rods around the rim. Finite mirror polygons, transparent media, and optical dispersion require their own path and propagation assumptions before using an exact formula.
An exact dimensionless check takes ΩR/c=1/5. Relative to L/c, the laboratory arrival times are 5/4 and 5/6, giving Δt/(L/c)=5/12. The detector instead records Δτ/(L/c)=6​/6≃0.408248. The leading Sagnac area law would give Δt/(L/c)≃2/5. These are model values chosen to make the relativistic distinction visible, not attainable parameters of the historical apparatus.
The rotating loop does not constitute a universal measurement of the one-way speed of light. It compares completed circuits at a single readout; assigning a velocity to each remote leg additionally requires a clock synchronization convention. Local Einstein synchronisation around a rotating rim does not close into a single globally synchronized clock network: the accumulated mismatch is another expression of the rotating-path asymmetry. Local comoving vacuum measurements still give c in both directions. Special relativity predicts a nonzero closed-loop delay because the receiver moves during propagation, while no single comoving inertial frame covers the whole circuit.

Four-vector (Uμ)

Words: 345 Articles: 5
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
A four-vector is a vector whose four vector components transform under a Lorentz transformation as U′μ=Λμν​Uν. Its individual vector components generally change between inertial frames; the Minkowski metric combines them into invariant scalar products. Listing four quantities is not enough to make a four-vector: their transformation law matters.
The most direct example is the displacement between two spacetime events, written (cΔt,Δx,Δy,Δz). Multiplying the time difference by the speed of light gives all four vector components the same length units. A position four-vector describes an event relative to a chosen origin, while a displacement does not depend on a common translation of the origin. Four-momentum and four-velocity use the same transformation rule for different physical quantities.

Minkowski spacetime (R1,3)

Words: 2k Articles: 21
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Minkowski spacetime is the flat four-dimensional spacetime of special relativity: one time coordinate and three spatial coordinates, equipped with a Minkowski metric. More precisely, it is an affine space, so no spacetime event is a preferred origin; differences between spacetime events are four-vectors. Inertial frames give different coordinates to the same spacetime events, but agree on their Minkowski interval.
This geometry answers two different measurement questions with one structure. Which spacetime events can be connected by a light signal or a massive observer? The light cone classifies them. How much time does a moving clock record? Its world line and the Minkowski metric determine its proper time. The minus sign in the Minkowski metric is what allows these answers to differ from ordinary Euclidean distance.
For a concrete one-space-dimensional slice, start at the origin O and measure t in seconds and x in light-seconds. The spacetime event A at (t,x)=(4s,3ls) can be reached by an observer moving at 0.75c, whereas B=(2s,3ls) would require 1.5c to be reached directly from O. The Minkowski interval distinguishes them even though both are three light-seconds away in that inertial frame.
Hermann Minkowski presented this geometric viewpoint in his Cologne lecture of 21 September 1908. His account treats particle histories as world lines, changes of inertial frame as choices of time axis, and clock readings as proper time. These are connected geometric ideas, rather than separate corrections to ordinary mechanics.[ref]

Minkowski spacetime OurBigBook.com
With the mostly-plus metric signature (−,+,+,+) and coordinates Xμ=(ct,x,y,z), the Minkowski metric is the nondegenerate bilinear form
ημν​=diag(−1,1,1,1),U⋅V=−U0V0+U1V1+U2V2+U3V3.

It is a symmetric bilinear form, but not a positive-definite bilinear form. For example, U=(1,1,0,0) is nonzero yet U⋅U=0, making it a null vector. This does not make the Minkowski metric degenerate: some other vectors have nonzero pairing with U.

(51)
For a timelike curve, a clock records dτ=−ds2​/c. For a null curve, ds2=0. For spacelike separation, the positive Minkowski interval measures a different kind of separation. A Lorentz transformation preserves this form, expressed in matrix notation by ΛTηΛ=η, although it need not preserve ordinary Euclidean distance in the four-component coordinate list.

The squared interval between two events in Minkowski spacetime is the quadratic form of their coordinate difference under the Minkowski metric. In signature (−,+,+,+) it is −c2Δt2+∣Δx∣2. Light cone (∣x∣2=c2t2)

Words: 546 Articles: 6
Minkowski metric OurBigBook.com
The light cone of a spacetime event O consists of O together with the spacetime events having null separation from it. In the coordinates of an inertial frame centered on O, it obeys
∣x∣2=c2t2.
(52)
For t>0 it traces an expanding spherical flash of light, with radius ct at time t; for t<0 it describes possible incoming light rays. A spacetime diagram with one spatial coordinate shows the two lines x=±ct. The apparent 45∘ angle uses equal scales for x and ct and is not a separate physical angle.
The light cone is the boundary, while its interior has timelike separation from O. An outgoing light ray follows the boundary; a future-directed massive observer's world line remains inside it. The exterior has spacelike separation: no signal travelling at or below the speed of light can connect its spacetime events directly to O. This separates possible causal influence from merely being assigned a later coordinate time.
In the diagram, A=(4s,3ls) is inside the future boundary, N=(3s,3ls) is on it, and B=(2s,3ls) is outside. Their squared Minkowski intervals are respectively −7,0,5 in ls2. Thus B occurs later than O in the displayed inertial frame while still being unable to receive a light-speed-or-slower signal sent from O.
The usefulness is immediate for an experiment: a detector's reading can depend on a source event only if a causal influence can reach it. A Lorentz boost changes coordinates but preserves this classification. For a boost with β=0.8 and Lorentz factor γ=5/3, applying the Lorentz transformation gives, in light-second length units,
(ct,x)A​=(4,3)(ct,x)N​=(3,3)(ct,x)B​=(2,3)​⟼(ct′,x′)A​=(8/3,−1/3),⟼(ct′,x′)N​=(1,1),⟼(ct′,x′)B​=(−2/3,7/3).​
(53)
The corresponding squared Minkowski intervals remain −7,0,5. In particular B is now earlier than O, which is allowed for spacelike separation; A remains later.

For a photon and a massive particle with zero total momentum, their momenta are opposite and equal. Conservation of total energy fixes the same momentum magnitude before and after elastic scattering, independently of direction. A right-angle photon turn therefore makes the recoiling particle move perpendicular to the original photon direction in that frame. Transform both velocity components, or the complete four-momentum, to obtain the laboratory recoil; a transverse component is reduced by the boost Lorentz factor when the particle has zero longitudinal velocity in the zero-momentum frame.

Four-momentum conservation OurBigBook.com

In the centre-of-momentum frame, total final energy is a sum of μi2​c4+c2∣pi​∣2​, each at least its rest energy. For massive products equality occurs with all at rest in that frame. A single product requires equality of the entire invariant mass, not just an inequality; a massless product cannot have nonzero energy and be at rest.

Applying the relativistic collision mass threshold gives the displayed necessary condition. The incoming energy must also satisfy E1​≥m1​c2; other conserved quantum numbers or reaction dynamics can impose further restrictions.

The massive multi-product threshold is the displayed value when ∑i​μi​>m2​. If the algebraic bound is nonpositive, the lower limit of allowed positive frequencies can be zero. Photon fixed-target production threshold OurBigBook.com
For a photon incident on a stationary electron, producing an additional electron and positron leaves three massive particles in the final state. Photon fixed-target production threshold OurBigBook.com
A photon hitting a resting mass m has squared total energy invariant m2c4+2mc2E. Producing a larger mass M and an outgoing photon requires this invariant to exceed M2c4 if the photon has positive energy. The displayed threshold is therefore the limiting infimum as the final photon becomes soft, not an attained physical state with a zero-energy photon. Above threshold the outgoing photon energy in the centre-of-momentum frame is positive.

Four-momentum conservation OurBigBook.com
An incident particle of rest mass m and energy E striking a stationary identical target has total squared invariant energy W2=2mc2(E+mc2). Producing N≥2 final particles of the same rest mass requires W≥Nmc2, giving the threshold. Equality means no final kinetic energy in the centre-of-momentum frame. From the Lorentz factor, the corresponding incident speed is at least cNN2−4​/(N2−2).

Four-momentum conservation OurBigBook.com
When an electron of Lorentz factor γ>1 annihilates with a stationary equal-mass positron, transverse four-momentum conservation makes the photons' transverse components opposite. Eliminating their positive frequencies gives the displayed relation for noncollinear photon angles to the incoming electron. The exactly collinear forward/backward configuration is physically allowed but makes the quotient 0/0; its undivided cross-multiplied identity remains valid. The angle relation thus requires nondegeneracy or an appropriate limit, rather than an assertion that every allowed angle pair defines the quotient.

Four-momentum conservation OurBigBook.com
When two massive particles coalesce without additional outgoing radiation, four-momentum conservation makes the final four-momentum their sum. For collinear incident velocities, its rest mass is the positive square root of the displayed invariant, and its final velocity equals the center-of-momentum frame velocity c2ptotal​/Etotal​. Relative kinetic energy can become internal rest energy, so the final rest mass is generally larger than the sum of the incident rest masses.

Invariant mass OurBigBook.com
Adding two null photon four-momenta gives the displayed invariant mass, with opening angle θ measured in the same frame as the energies. A nonzero mass of the pair does not give either photon a rest mass. At fixed energies it vanishes for parallel photons and is greatest for opposite directions. A reconstructed mass peak must be assessed with background, resolution and identification controls before assigning a parent particle.

Angular errors, if present, add the corresponding derivative and covariance terms.

The mass ordering is mC​>mB​>mA​>0. spin correlations can alter the distribution inside these limits, but cannot move the kinematic endpoints while the same on-shell decay chain applies.

Thus mAt2​ has minimum mA2​mC2​/mB2​ and maximum mA2​+mC2​−mB2​, attained at the opposite relative angles from the s,t pair endpoints. Mass threshold after photon absorption (M2=m2+2mE/c2)

Words: 69
Relativistic two-body decay OurBigBook.com
A stationary particle of rest mass m absorbing a photon of energy E acquires total invariant mass
M=m2+2mE/c2​.

This follows from four-momentum conservation, since the incoming photon has momentum magnitude E/c. If the system splits into two equal particles, the largest kinematically permitted daughter rest mass is M/2, attained when both are at rest in the centre-of-momentum frame. Their common laboratory speed at threshold is cE/(mc2+E). Above this daughter-mass threshold there is insufficient centre-of-momentum energy; below it, relative kinetic energy is available.

Words: 65
Mandelstam variables OurBigBook.com
With a specified ordering of external legs, this crossed channel carries the difference between an incoming and an outgoing energy-momentum vector. A one-particle exchange pole requires that difference to be on the exchanged particle's mass shell. Ordered amplitudes in one spatial dimension can label the crossed invariant using the difference of the two rapidity-parameterized external momenta; the external-leg convention fixes which crossed invariant is named t.

The direct channel combines the two incoming four-momentum vectors. A one-particle pole in this channel has the intermediate particle's squared mass equal to s. Imaginary rapidity differences can satisfy this mass relation for a bound state even though there is no pole at real physical scattering rapidity.

A massive observer's four-velocity is the tangent Uμ=dXμ/dτ to its worldline, parametrized by proper time. Its invariant squared Minkowski norm is c2 in the +−−− metric signature, and −c2 in the opposite convention. Unlike the coordinate values Xμ, the tangent transforms as a vector under a general coordinate change.

Special relativity OurBigBook.com
The four-acceleration is the covariant derivative of four-velocity along a massive observer's worldline: Aμ=dUμ/dτ+Γνρμ​UνUρ. In Cartesian Minkowski spacetime coordinates the Christoffel symbols vanish, leaving the ordinary proper time derivative. Differentiating the constant velocity norm gives U⋅A=0; in the instantaneous rest frame, A=(0,a), so A⋅A=−a2 with +−−− metric signature. The magnitude a is the proper acceleration.

The instantaneous spatial acceleration is perpendicular to velocity, even though the particle has nonzero proper acceleration.

A uniformly accelerated observer has a null boundary beyond which light signals can never reach the observer.

Equating it to the emission value te​−L gives the displayed reception relation. Differentiating yields the Doppler frequency ratio ν/ν0​=dte​/dτ=e−aτ. The limiting emission time L is a supremum: emission exactly at that time is never received at finite proper time. These expressions use c=1 and acceleration continued indefinitely.

Let an observer start at rest at T=0, X=R=c2/a and accelerate towards increasing X with constant proper acceleration a>0. A signal emitted simultaneously from X=R−d travels along X=R−d+cT. The observer follows hyperbolic motion, X=Rcosh(aτ/c) and cT=Rsinh(aτ/c). Their intersection obeys

In units c=1, a receiver on the hyperbolic motion worldline t=a−1sinh(aτ), x=a−1cosh(aτ) has retarded null coordinate p=t−x=−a−1e−aτ. The photon wave covector is proportional to (1,−1), and contraction with the receiver's four-velocity gives its measured frequency as ν0​(t˙−x˙)=ν0​e−aτ. Relativistic causality

Words: 65 Articles: 2
Special relativity OurBigBook.com
Relativistic causality requires physical influences and controllable information to propagate only within or on the future light cone of their source.

Spacelike separation

Words: 27
Relativistic causality OurBigBook.com
Two events are spacelike separated when no signal traveling at or below the speed of light can connect them. Their temporal order can differ between inertial frames.

Faster-than-light communication

Words: 17
Relativistic causality OurBigBook.com
Superluminal signalling would transmit controllable information outside the source event's future light cone and would violate relativistic causality.
